technique: sound — the consonants and vowels doing quiet work, worth saying aloud
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: sound. Sound means the way the consonants and vowels feel in your mouth when you say them, apart from what the words mean.

This poem uses repeated letter sounds. Listen for "the slow heat is building"—the "s" and "l" sounds come back and make the line move slowly when you say it. Then "bare arms working the gray"—the hard "r" sound shows up three times. And "a whole day's worth of tending"—the soft "w" and "th" sounds are gentle, and they slow you down.

It works because repeated sounds make a line harder or easier to say out loud. That change in effort is something your ear picks up, even when you don't notice why.

Try this: say your line out loud and repeat one sound two or three times, then keep it if it fits the feeling.

The second time through, listen for which letter sounds come back. Here is the poem.
poem:
The fog that slept all night along the low ground
is standing up now, going where the wind tells it,
and the hills come back one dark ridge at a time.
The maples have let go—bare arms working the gray,
that patient creaking a man could mistake for his own.
A little rain still hangs in the air, not falling,
just waiting, the way a thought waits to be finished.
The kettle wants watching. The dog wants out.
And somewhere the slow heat is building in a covered pot,
a whole day's worth of tending you've already set in motion.
You slept a few hours and the work went on without asking.
Now it's yours again, this close and ordinary hour—

Step outside—the cold air's waiting
to wake you better than I can.
